newsitem.title: UK: Sterling powers to new highs above three marks.
newsitem.headline: Sterling powers to new highs above three marks.

text.p: Sterling vaulted above three marks for the first time in more than 6-1/2 years on Friday as traders proved unable to resist the lure of higher British interest rates.
"Economists are getting trampled in the rush," said Mark Cliffe, chief international economist at HSBC Markets.
"They can say the pound is overvalued for all they are worth but all traders can see is pound signs as rates are going higher."
Its surge encountered little resistance from the Bank of England, according to traders, who said there was no sign yet of any central bank intervention to halt its rally.
The pound rose to 3.0010 marks, the strongest it has been since October 1990. It was at 2.9965/75 at 1435 GMT from 2.9566/76 late Thursday in Europe.
Against the dollar, it reached $1.6986, its strongest since January 10. It was last at $1.6967/78 from $1.6882/92 on Thursday.
The pound's trade-weighted index climbed to its highest since October 1990.
Initial market disappointment that interest rates rose by only a quarter percentage point on Thursday proved short-lived, given expectations that more increases are on the way.
This made the psychological target of three marks to the pound an irresistible magnet for short-term traders.

"The market has come to its senses and realised that a quarter point rate rise yesterday does not preclude more rate rises, probably substantial ones," said Steve Hannah, the director of economic research at IBJ International.
"It is difficult to see sterling backing down even from three marks."

A potent cocktail of strong consumption data, a budget which was viewed as being too soft on consumers and an increase in the government's preferred measure of inflation have fuelled the latest stretch of sterling's rally.
"The budget did not do enough on the consumer side," said Ian Winship, a fund manager at Scottish Amicable Investment Managers in Glasgow. "The Bank of England has no choice but to raise rates."
At 6.75 percent, base lending rates are already the highest of any major industrial nation and above most European Union rates.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer indicated on Thursday that policy makers outside Britain viewed sterling's rise as justified. He said the pound's strength reflected economic fundamentals and interest rate expectations.
The premium that British government bonds offer over their EU counterparts is also beginning to look attractive.
British bonds have failed to keep pace with gains that Italian and Spanish bonds have scored amid expectations that a broad group of countries will launch European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Expectations that Britain will not join EMU from the outset may have handicapped the British bond market but they have benefited sterling.

Concern that the planned European single currency will not be as strong as the mark and the fact that the pound is not tied to the mark in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism have helped the pound climb against a broad range of currencies.
Its trade-weighted index has surged 24 percent since August.
This strength may eventually prove to be sterling's undoing, though, some analysts warned.
The damage it is inflicting on exporters will eventually boost Britain's trade deficit and could force the central bank to intervene in the open market to curb its strength, they said.
But traders are not yet concerned.

"The Bank has to do something to stop sterling's rise but it probably does not want to show its hand at the moment," a London-based trader said. "Also, they will have learnt their lesson from years past and will not want to take the market on aggressively."
A bigger risk for sterling could be concern that German officials are beginning to voice about the mark's slump against the dollar.

Also, longer-term investors are wary of piling in after a year-long rally which has boosted sterling by 30 percent against the mark. This leaves sterling vulnerable to quick reversals in short-term trading sentiment.
"I'd rather not buy gilts or sterling for my overseas accounts right now as I'm too nervous about it swinging around," said Winship."
